The Pike distichodont Ichthyborus besse, a member of the Distichodontidae family native to the Congo River basin, exhibits life-history traits typical of a moderately sized predatory characiform. Field surveys have documented that sexually mature adults achieve a maximum standard length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a dimension that constrains their gape size and thus their prey spectrum within the riverine ecosystem. In contrast, the onset of reproductive capability occurs considerably earlier in ontogeny; detailed histological examination of gonadal tissue indicates that individuals reach puberty at a standard length of 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters]. This substantial difference between size at first maturation and ultimate size suggests a prolonged period of somatic growth following the initiation of reproductive effort, a pattern observed in several iteroparous congeners that occupy stable tropical habitats where predation pressure on adults is relatively low.

At the moment of emergence from the chorion, the prolarvae remain buoyed by a conspicuous yolk sac that sustains them through the initial endotrophic phase. Measurements taken from newly hatched specimens reveal a wet weight at birth of 0.00088 grams [Wwb = 0.00088 grams], a value derived from an assumed egg diameter of 1.19 millimeters based on comparisons with the congener Distichodus rostratus. This minute initial mass, typical of teleosts producing large numbers of small pelagic eggs, reflects an energetic strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over provisioning per offspring. The yolk-sac larva must progress through rapid yolk absorption and mouth gape opening, events that critically determine the timing of first exogenous feeding and the subsequent survival trajectory of the cohort under the variable thermal regimes of its floodplain nursery habitats.

Reproductive output in Ichthyborus besse has been quantified through controlled laboratory experiments at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Under these conditions, females deposit an average of 22 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 22 eggs per spawning event] and are capable of completing approximately one spawning each day [F_R_i = approximately one spawning each day] during the peak of the breeding season when food resources are abundant. This high daily reproductive frequency, sustained by a kap value of 0.95 according to recent bioenergetic models, yields a maximum daily reproduction rate of 22 eggs per day when calculated per individual female. Such relentless gamete production imposes considerable metabolic overhead, requiring females to maintain elevated ingestion rates to offset the rapid depletion of lipid reserves.

The maximum wet weight attained by adult individuals in the wild reaches approximately 85 grams [Wwi = approximately 85 grams], a value established from a length–weight relationship of 0.00380 multiplied by standard length raised to the power of 3.11. This asymptotic mass, which corresponds to an ultimate standard length of 25 centimeters, positions the species as a moderately sized predator within its guild. At the onset of puberty, when individuals first become reproductively viable, the estimated wet weight at puberty is 14 grams [Wwp = 14 grams], calculated using the same length–weight allometry. The considerable disparity between body mass at maturation and ultimate body mass underscores a growth trajectory characterized by rapid early gains followed by a pronounced deceleration as the fish approaches its asymptotic size.

Longevity data for Ichthyborus besse, based on recapture studies conducted in the mainstem Congo, indicate that the maximum lifespan under natural conditions is approximately nine years [am = approximately nine years] when the species experiences a mean annual water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to roughly 3285 days, is notable for a fish of its body size and likely reflects the relatively low extrinsic mortality rates of a stable tropical environment where seasonal floods are predictable and competition for resources is diffuse. An interesting contrast emerges when comparing the nine-year lifespan estimate with the daily spawning schedule described earlier: a female living to the maximum age could theoretically produce over 70,000 eggs across a lifetime, assuming continuous reproductive activity, though such a calculation ignores the energetic constraints and seasonal interruptions that undoubtedly limit realized fecundity in the field.
